Look, teacher—let’s explain the MACD simply.

MACD compares moving averages and shows whether momentum is changing or if it’s still continuing.
We use it to benefit when a crossover happens with a clear direction, especially after consolidation—not right after a huge candle.

The biggest mistake: a crossover by itself isn’t an entry signal. In a sideways market, it produces many signals with no real value.

Quick example: if the price breaks above resistance and MACD starts improving and volume increases, then following through here makes sense.

This time’s follow-up angle: if you’re going to track the trade, scale it in stages.

The indicator alone isn’t enough. Pair it with the trend, volume, support, and resistance—then your decision will be calmer and cleaner.

Europe Pays to Reopen the Strait of Hormuz! Can BTC $64,330 Still Hold Up?

💡 Bearish Warning: Geopolitical risk is being shifted onto Europe, and risk-hedging sentiment is actually heating up—suppressing risk assets.

In plain terms, the market’s uncertainty has just been added to. BTC is currently quoted at $64,330.37, up only 0.58% in 24h. ETH is at $1,877.19, up 0.29%—this kind of move is nowhere near enough to matter.

According to a report by The Telegraph, Europe is weighing a plan to gather money to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. This sounds like it’s meant to clear risks for the global energy supply chain and stabilize oil prices. Back then, the U.S. usually took the lead—sending warships and handling it. Now Europe wants to pay for it itself and weaken Iran’s strategic leverage over this waterway. But the problem is, this plan is still just a “dinner-table talk” stage, and nobody knows whether it can actually be implemented.

Short term, this piece of news is definitely not good for the crypto market. On the surface, reopening the strait might stabilize oil. But what the capital sees is the complex nature of the U.S.-Europe standoff in the Middle East. Capital hates uncertainty the most. Once Europe truly throws real money into it, it’s essentially an admission that the situation has deteriorated to the point where money is needed to patch the hole. That’s similar to what happens with safe-haven assets: funds get drained out of the high-risk crypto market and instead flow into gold and U.S. Treasuries. In the past few days, BTC has only moved about 0.58%, which suggests big money is still watching from the sidelines—no one wants to catch a falling knife right now.

Medium term, if energy prices swing sharply due to delays in the agreement, inflation expectations will likely flare up again. Once the hope for Fed rate cuts is shattered, the valuation logic in crypto will have to be marked down further.

My view is very clear: bearish. The $64,330.37 support line for BTC is simply not solid. As soon as you hear even a small piece of news that a European plan at the Hormuz side has hit a negotiation wall, it could quickly break through to the downside. ETH at $1,877.19 is also risky. With macro conditions dragging along, it likely needs to probe lower as well. Don’t rush in to buy the dip now. If you really want to act, you should wait for a second dip and stabilization. Big money is watching—why are retail traders rushing?

Federal Reserve Chair Powell floated an idea at last week’s policy meeting: compress the regular monetary policy meetings held eight times a year down to six, with the other two converted into short meetings that would cover only a single specific economic issue. He did not solicit discussion on the spot, but instead asked officials to provide feedback separately afterward. The new schedule could be finalized before the next meeting in mid-September.

This eight-meeting cadence was set by Volcker in 1981 and has been used for 45 years. The 1935 Banking Act only requires at least four meetings per year, and the chair or any three commissioners can temporarily convene additional meetings. Meeting fewer times doesn’t mean there is no capacity for emergency action.

More than two months into his tenure, his moves have consistently pointed in the same direction: the post-meeting statement has been greatly scaled back, forward guidance has been removed, and the number of press conferences is also being considered for cuts. In 2014, when Carney asked him to assess the Bank of England’s transparency, the advice he gave was to reduce the number of meetings from 12 to eight, arguing that economic judgments within a four-week span rarely change much.

For the $BTC  and $ETH  who never close their markets around the clock, what changes isn’t the interest rate—it’s the rhythm. With fewer meetings and less guidance, the gaps stretch out, and the moment CPI, PCE, and Nonfarm Payrolls are released becomes the pricing window.

Look, my teacher—let’s explain the MACD simply.

MACD compares moving averages and shows whether momentum is changing or if it’s still continuing.
We use it to take advantage when it gets a crossover with a clear direction, especially after a calm period—not right after a huge candle.

Most important mistake: a crossover by itself isn’t an entry signal. In a sideways market you’ll get many crossovers that don’t mean much.

Quick example: if the price breaks above resistance, and at the same time MACD starts improving and volume increases, then following through becomes logical.

The follow-up angle this time: if the picture isn’t clear, missing the opportunity is a respectable decision.

The indicator alone isn’t enough. Pair it with the trend, volume, support, and resistance—then the decision becomes calmer and cleaner.

Look, boss—let’s explain RSI simply.

This is a momentum indicator: it tells you whether the move is strong or starting to get tired.
We use it to spot situations where if RSI rises along with the price, the momentum is helping; but if the price rises while RSI weakens, watch out for divergence.

The biggest mistake: the worst thing you can do is sell just because RSI is above 70, or buy just because it’s below 30. You must check the trend first.

Quick example: if the coin is in an uptrend and RSI falls back from 50 and then climbs again, that’s a stronger continuation signal than randomly entering near 30.

This time’s follow-up angle: split the trade into stages if you’re going to continue.
